title: Learning Agility
summary: Learn new tools quickly using a fast-learning method, the Feynman technique, deliberate practice and a short learning plan.
objectives: Break a new tool down into a map of core ideas.
Use the Feynman technique to find gaps.
Write a two-week learning plan with practice.

explanation.heading: Learning how to learn
explanation.body: In a first job you will repeatedly meet new tools: a version control system, a testing framework, a new module. Your speed at getting competent matters as much as what you already know. **Learning agility** is the ability to pick up new skills quickly and apply them. It comes from a few methods you can practise: map the territory, test your understanding by explaining it, practise on real tasks and plan your time.

explanation.heading: Map the territory first
explanation.body: Before details, draw a **learning map** on one page: what is this tool for, what are its five to ten core concepts and how do they connect? For an unfamiliar SAP transaction or a new framework, find the official overview, a beginner tutorial and one real example. List the concepts, then rank them by how often you will use them. The 20% of features that cover 80% of daily work come first. Keep a glossary of new terms. Skip advanced features until you can complete a basic task from start to end. Beginners often feel pressure to master everything at once; resist it. A narrow but working skill gives you something to build on and shows your team you can already contribute, while the rest can be learned on the job as real needs appear.

explanation.heading: The Feynman technique
explanation.body: The **Feynman technique** tests whether you really understand something. Step one: choose a concept. Step two: explain it in simple words as if to a beginner, in writing or aloud, without jargon. Step three: note where you stumble or fall back on technical words; these are the gaps. Step four: go back to the source, fill the gap and explain again. If you cannot explain a concept simply, you do not yet understand it. A rubber duck, a friend or a voice memo all work as audiences.

explanation.heading: Practice loop and learning plan
explanation.body: Learning sticks through use. Use a **practice loop**: try a small task, check the result, fix errors and repeat with a slightly harder task. Mix in **retrieval**, such as writing a command from memory before looking it up. Then build a **learning plan** for two weeks: a target ("create and test a simple report program"), daily 45-minute sessions with a single focus, one small project to apply it and a checkpoint at day seven where you demonstrate what you can do. Share progress with someone, because explaining what you did makes you notice what you skipped. Write a two-line note at the end of each session: what I learned and what is still unclear. These notes become your own reference guide. If you are stuck for more than 25 minutes, ask for help; hiding confusion slows you down.

examples.title: A one-page map
examples.body: To learn Git, Ashish lists: repository, commit, branch, merge, remote. He ranks commit and branch first, completes a small project using only those and learns merge later when he needs it.
examples.takeaway: Start with the few concepts used most.

examples.title: A Feynman gap
examples.body: Asked to explain an index in a database, Leena says "it makes lookups faster using a structure". When asked how, she cannot answer. She reads about B-trees, then explains it as the index at the back of a book.
examples.takeaway: Stumbling reveals what to study next.

exercises.prompt: What should you learn first about a new tool?
options: The few core concepts used most often
exercises.why: Core, frequently used concepts give the fastest start.

exercises.prompt: The Feynman technique asks you to explain a concept in ____ words. (one word)
exercises.why: If you cannot explain it simply, you have a gap.

exercises.prompt: Choose a tool or skill you want to learn. Write a two-week plan: the target outcome, the daily 45-minute focus for the first three days, one small project, and a day-seven checkpoint.
exercises.modelAnswer: Target: write and run three SQL queries with joins on a sample database. Day 1: tables and primary keys. Day 2: INNER JOIN with two tables. Day 3: LEFT JOIN and NULLs. Project: a student marks database with five tables. Day 7 checkpoint: solve six join problems without notes and explain two aloud.
exercises.guidance: Strong plans have a testable outcome, small daily steps, a real project and a checkpoint. Avoid plans that only list topics.

task.title: Learn something in 45 minutes
task.brief: Pick a small tool or feature and learn it using the map, Feynman and a practice task.
steps: Draw a one-page map with five concepts.
Explain the main concept aloud in simple words and note gaps.
Write what you will do tomorrow to fill the gaps.
